editorial_contributions.text: This is a review paper on soap bubbles and minimal surfaces written by one of the leading experts on the topic. The paper is addressed to a wide audience, not only scholars. It contains several images describing some kinds of soap bubbles and in particular one image shows how human cells look and act like soap bubbles.

editorial_contributions.text: The general soap bubble problem looks for a least-area way to enclose and separate a number of given volumes in \(\mathbb{R}^ n\) or in a smooth compact Riemannian manifold. Existence and regularity were treated by F. Almgren \((n \geq 3)\) and J. Taylor \((n = 3)\). The present paper proves the corresponding result in dimension 2: the solutions consist of constant- curvature arcs meeting in threes at 120 degrees. If the combinatorial type is described, too, then the arcs may bump up against each other.

editorial_contributions.text: The paper is a survey of several open questions in the geometry of soap bubbles. In particular the author considers the problem: do soap bubble clusters always find the absolute least area shape? The answer is: not always. Several figures illustrate open questions like: for area- minimizing clusters, it is an open question whether each separate region is connected. It is an open question too whether an area-minimizing cluster may incidentally trap inside ``empy chambers'' which do not contribute to the prescribed volume. The planar soap bubble problem is considered: find the least perimeter way to enclose and separate \(n\) given areas in the plane. All problems are illustrated by figures and the results are not proved in the paper but references are given. The authors point out the importance of undergraduate research groups in mathematics quoting results obtained by the Williams College SMALL undergraduate research project in the area of geometry of soap bubbles.

editorial_contributions.text:
The author is presenting to a general audience the main ideas of the geometry of soap bubbles and soap films. He recalls the discovery of the behaviour of singularities obtained by the Belgian physicist J. A. F. Plateau and the famous demonstration of Plateau's results obtained by Jean E. Taylor, in 1976 [\textit{J. E. Taylor}, Ann. Math. (2) 103, 489--539 (1976; Zbl 0335.49032)]. Then he poses the question: Can a boundary support infinitely many soap films? Richard Courant described an example in 1950 that he himself considered so badly twisted [\textit{R. Courant}, Dirichlet's principle, conformal mapping and minimal surfaces. New York: Interscience Publishers (1950; Zbl 0040.34603), p. 122]. The author asks himself a similar question: Can a nice, smooth boundary support infinitely many soap films?


The answer is yes and he describes how to construct the example. The boundary consists of four wires bent into four circles. Two of the circles are concentric; a third circle lies between and above them, and a fourth circle lies between and below them. One soap film with its boundary consists of two separate strips of surface, each bounded by two of the circles. Another soap film consists of strips that switch at two crosspiece saddles placed at opposite points and balancing each other. There can be any even number of evenly spaced crosspiece saddles and holes in a soap film that looks something like the original figure 12 in the paper. Then any one such soap film gives rise to infinitely many others under rotations. The proof, a sketch of the proof, is given using the reflection principle and the figures. It is a visual demonstration and so illustrations are really essential. A detailed version of the proof appeared [the author, Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal. 75, 193--197 (1981; Zbl 0453.49027)]. The illustrations are by Jim Bredt.


[For the entire collection see Zbl 0742.00037.]

editorial_contributions.text: On a Riemannian surface there is a curve, often of constant curvature, which minimizes length among all curves bounding the same area or curvature. This curve can be required to satisfy additional topological restrictions. One consequence is a simple proof of an argument, suggested by Poincaré, that the shortest curve which divides a convex 2-sphere into two regions of total curvature \(2\pi\) is a simple geodesic.

editorial_contributions.text:
Planar soap bubble froths have bubbles that meet in at most three at a point whereas in dimension three typically at most four bubbles meet. 

In this paper it is shown that it is not possible to decompose the \(n\)-dimensional space \({\mathbb R}^n\) into sets of bounded diameter where at most \(n\) such sets meet. The base is Lebesgue's covering theorem which says that it is impossible to decompose the unit cube in \({\mathbb R}^n\) into pieces of diameter less than 1 so that at most \(n\) pieces meet at a point. Among other corollaries the authors prove the following: There is no decomposition of the unit \(n\)-ball of \({\mathbb R}^n\) into sets of diameter less than \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{n}}\) that meet at most \(n\) at a point. Consequently, if a 3-dimensional soap bubble cluster covers a ball of diameter at least \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) times the largest diameter of a bubble in the cluster, then there must be a point where four bubbles meet.
